{{Short description|Discrete phenomenon that exists at a location on Earth}}
 
In [[geography]] and particularly in [[geographic information science]], a '''geographic feature''' or simply '''feature''' (also called an '''object''' or '''entity''') is a representation of phenomenon that exists at a location in the [[space]] and scale of relevance to [[geography]]; that is, at or near the surface of [[Earth]].<ref name="longley2015">{{cite book |last1=Longley |first1=Paul A. |last2=Goodchild |first2=Michael F. |last3=Maguire |first3=David J. |last4=Rhind |first4=David W. |title=Geographic Information Systems & Science |date=2015 |publisher=Wiley |edition=4th}}</ref>{{rp|page=62}}<ref name="x204">{{cite web | title=MLGT: The authoritative multi-lingual geographic information terminology database | website=geographic feature | date=2023-12-13 | url=https://isotc211.geolexica.org/concepts/203/ | access-date=2024-12-11}}</ref> It is an item of [[geographic information]], and may be represented in [[map]]s, [[geographic information system]]s, [[remote sensing]] imagery, [[spatial analysis|statistics]], and other forms of geographic discourse. Such representations of phenomena consist of descriptions of their inherent nature, their spatial form and location, and their characteristics or properties.<ref name="mennis2000">{{cite journal |last1=Mennis |first1=Jeremy |last2=Peuquet |first2=Donna J. |last3=Qian |first3=L. |title=A geographical database representation |journal=International Journal of Geographical Information Science |date=2000 |volume=14 |issue=6 |pages=501–520 |doi=10.1080/136588100415710|s2cid=7458359 }}</ref>

==Terminology==
The term "feature" is broad and inclusive, and includes both [[list of natural phenomena|natural]] and human-constructed objects. The term covers things which exist physically (e.g. a [[building]]) as well as those that are conceptual or social creations (e.g. a [[neighbourhood]]). Formally, the term is generally restricted to things which endure over a period. A feature is also discrete, meaning that it has a clear identity and location distinct from other objects, and is defined as a whole, defined more or less precisely by the boundary of its geographical extent. This differentiates features from geographic [[process theory|processes]] and [[event (philosophy)|events]], which are [[Formal ontology#perdurant|perdurants]] that only exist in time{{clarify|date=September 2023}}; and from geographic masses and [[field (geography)|fields]], which are ''continuous'' in that they are not conceptualized as a distinct whole.<ref name="plewe2019">{{cite book |last1=Plewe |first1=Brandon |editor1-last=Timpf |editor1-first=S. |editor2-last=Schlieder |editor2-first=C. |editor3-last=Kattenbeck |editor3-first=M. |editor4-last=Ludwig |editor4-first=B. |editor5-last=Stewart |editor5-first=K. |title=14th International Conference on Spatial Information Theory (COSIT 2019) |date=2019 |publisher=Schloss Dagstuhl-Leibniz-Zentrum fuer Informatik |pages=14:1–14 |chapter=A Case for Geographic Masses|series=Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics (LIPIcs) |volume=142 |doi=10.4230/LIPIcs.COSIT.2019.14|doi-access=free |isbn=9783959771153 }}</ref>

In [[geographic information science]], the terms ''feature'', ''object'', and ''entity'' are generally used as roughly [[synonym]]ous. In the 1992 [[Spatial Data Transfer Standard]] (SDTS), one of the first public standard models of geographic information, an attempt was made to formally distinguish them: an ''entity'' as the real-world phenomenon, an ''object'' as a representation thereof (e.g. on [[paper]] or digital), and a ''feature'' as the combination of both entity and representation objects.<ref name="fegeas1992">{{cite journal |last1=Fegeas |first1=Robin G. |last2=Cascio |first2=Janette L. |last3=Lazar |first3=Robert A. |title=An Overview of FIPS 173, The Spatial Data Transfer Standard |journal=Cartography and Geographic Information Systems |date=1992 |volume=19 |issue=5 |pages=278–293 |doi=10.1559/152304092783762209|bibcode=1992CGISy..19..278F }}</ref> Although this distinction is often cited in textbooks, it has not gained lasting nor widespread usage. In the ISO 19101 Geographic Information Reference Model<ref>{{cite web |last1=International Standards Organization |title=ISO 19101-1:2014, Geographic Information-Reference Model-Part 1: Fundamentals |url=https://www.iso.org/standard/59164.html |website=ISO Standards}}</ref> and Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) [[Simple Features]] Specification,<ref>{{cite web |author=Open Geospatial Consortium |title=Simple Feature Access - Part 1: Common Architecture |url=https://www.ogc.org/standards/sfa |website=OGC Standards}}</ref> international standards that form the basis for most modern geospatial technologies, a ''feature'' is defined as "an abstraction of a real-world phenomenon", essentially the ''object'' in SDTS.

==Types of features==

===Natural features===
A natural feature is an object on the planet that was not created by humans, but is a part of the natural world.<ref>There has been some metaphysical debate over whether such features are "real", independent of the human mind (a [[philosophical realism|realist]] stance), whether they are purely human conceptualizations of continuous natural phenomena (a [[constructivism (philosophy of science)|constructivist]] stance), or a hybrid of discrete natural phenomena that highly motivate, but are simplified by human concepts (a [[experientialism|experientialist]] stance). It is also possible that individual features may be of any of these three types. {{cite book |last1=Frank |first1=Andrew U. |editor1-last=Sellis |editor1-first=Timos |title=Spatio-Temporal Databases: The Chorochronos Approach |date=2003 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |pages=9–77 |chapter=Ontology for Spatio-Temporal Databases|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=V.2520|doi=10.1007/978-3-540-45081-8_2|isbn=978-3-540-40552-8 }}</ref>

====Ecosystems ====
{{Main|Ecosystem}}

There are two different terms to describe [[habitat]]s: ecosystem and [[biome]]. An ecosystem is a community of organisms.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Odum|first1=Eugene P.|author-link1=Eugene Odum|last2=Odum|first2=Howard T.|author-link2=Howard Thomas Odum|title=Fundamentals of Ecology |url=https://archive.org/details/fundamentalsofec0000odum|url-access=registration|date=1971|publisher=[[Saunders (imprint)|Saunders]]|isbn=9780721669410 |edition=3rd}}</ref> In contrast, biomes occupy large areas of the globe and often encompass many different kinds of geographical features, including [[mountain range]]s.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Botkin|first1=Daniel B.|last2=Keller|first2=Edward A.|title=Environmental Science: Earth as a Living Planet|url=https://archive.org/details/environmentalsci00botk|url-access=registration|date=1995|publisher=John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Canada|isbn=9780471545484 }}</ref>

Biotic diversity within an ecosystem is the variability among living organisms from all sources, including ''[[List of Latin phrases (I)#inter alia|inter alia]]'', terrestrial, marine and other aquatic ecosystems.<ref>{{cite web|title=Convention Text — Article 2. Use of Terms|url=https://www.cbd.int/convention/articles/default.shtml?a=cbd-02|website=www.CBD.int| date=2 November 2006 |publisher=Convention on Biological Diversity|access-date=13 September 2015}}</ref> Living [[organism]]s are continually engaged in a set of relationships with every other element constituting the [[biophysical environment|environment]] in which they exist, and ecosystem describes any situation where there is relationship between organisms and their environment.

Biomes represent large areas of ecologically similar [[community (ecology)|communities]] of [[plant]]s, [[animal]]s, and soil organisms.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Basak|first1=Anindita|title=Environmental Studies|date=2009|publisher=[[Dorling Kindersley]]|isbn=978-81-317-2118-6|page=288|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yElrhPSIq-wC&pg=PA288|access-date=13 September 2015}}</ref> Biomes are defined based on factors such as plant structures (such as trees, shrubs, and grasses), leaf types (such as broadleaf and needleleaf), plant spacing (forest, woodland, savanna), and climate. Unlike [[biogeographic realm]]s, biomes are not defined by genetic, taxonomic, or historical similarities. Biomes are often identified with particular patterns of [[ecological succession]] and [[climax community|climax vegetation]].

====Water bodies====
{{Main|Hydrology}}

A body of water is any significant and reasonably long-lasting accumulation of water, usually covering the land. The term "body of water" most often refers to [[ocean]]s, [[sea]]s, and [[lake]]s, but it may also include smaller pools of water such as [[pond]]s, [[creek (tidal)|creeks]] or [[wetland]]s. [[River]]s, [[stream]]s, [[canal]]s, and other geographical features where water moves from one place to another are not always considered bodies of water, but they are included as geographical formations featuring water.

Some of these are easily recognizable as distinct real-world entities (e.g. an isolated lake), while others are at least partially based on human conceptualizations. Examples of the latter are a branching stream network in which one of the branches has been arbitrarily designated as the continuation of the primary named stream; or a [[gulf]] or [[bay]] of a body of water (e.g. a lake or an ocean), which has no meaningful dividing line separating it from the rest of the lake or ocean.

==== Landforms ====
{{Main|Landform}}

A landform comprises a [[geomorphology|geomorphological]] unit and is largely defined by its surface form and location in the landscape, as part of the [[terrain]], and as such is typically an element of [[topography]]. Landforms are categorized by features such as elevation, slope, orientation, [[stratum|stratification]], rock exposure, and soil type. They include [[berm]]s, [[mound]]s, hills, [[cliffs]], [[valleys]], [[river]]s, and numerous other elements. [[Ocean]]s and [[continent]]s are the highest-order landforms.

=== Artificial features ===
==== Settlements ====
{{Main|Human settlement}}

A settlement is a permanent or temporary [[community]] in which people live. Settlements range in components from a small number of dwellings grouped together to the largest of cities with surrounding urbanized areas. Other landscape features such as roads, enclosures, field systems, boundary banks and ditches, ponds, parks and woods, mills, manor houses, moats, and churches may be considered part of a settlement.<ref>{{cite web|title=MSRG Policy Statement|url=http://medieval-settlement.com/about/policy/|website=Medieval-Settlement.com|publisher=Medieval Settlement Research Group|access-date=13 September 2015|date=2014-05-11}}</ref>

==== Administrative regions and other constructs ====
These include social constructions that are created to administer and organize the land, people, and other spatially-relevant resources.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Montello |first1=Daniel R. |editor1-last=Duckham |editor1-first=Matthew |editor2-last=Goodchild |editor2-first=Michael F. |editor3-last=Worboys |editor3-first=Michael |title=Foundations of geographic information science |date=2003 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |pages=173–189 |chapter=Regions in geography: Process and content}}</ref> Examples are [[government|governmental units]] such as a [[state (polity)|state]], [[cadastre|cadastral land parcels]], [[mineral rights|mining claims]], [[zoning]] partitions of a city, and church [[parish]]es. There are also more informal social features, such as city neighbourhoods and other vernacular regions. These are purely conceptual entities established by [[edict]] or practice, although they may align with visible features (e.g. a river boundary), and may be subsequently manifested on the ground, such as by [[survey marker]]s or fences.

==== Engineered constructs ====
{{Main|Construction engineering|Building|Nonbuilding structure}}
{{See also|Infrastructure}}

Engineered geographic features include [[highway]]s, [[bridge]]s, [[airport]]s, [[railroad]]s, [[building]]s, [[dam]]s, and [[reservoir (water)|reservoirs]], and are part of the [[anthroposphere]] because they are man-made geographic features.

=== Cartographic features ===
{{Main|Cartography|Map}}

Cartographic features are types of abstract geographical features, which appear on maps but not on the planet itself, even though they are located on the planet. For example, grid lines, [[latitude]]s, [[longitude]]s, the [[Equator]], the [[prime meridian]], and many types of boundary, are shown on maps of Earth, but do not physically exist. They are theoretical lines used for reference, navigation, and measurement.

== Features and Geographic Information ==
{{seealso | Data model (GIS) }}
In GIS, maps, statistics, databases, and other information systems, a geographic feature is represented by a set of descriptors of its various characteristics. A common classification of those characteristics has emerged based on developments by Peuquet,<ref name="peuquet1994">{{cite journal |last1=Peuquet |first1=Donna J. |title=It's about time: a conceptual framework for the representation of temporal dynamics in geographic information systems |journal=Annals of the Association of American Geographers |date=1994 |volume=84 |issue=3 |pages=441–461|doi=10.1111/j.1467-8306.1994.tb01869.x }}</ref> Mennis,<ref name="mennis2000" /> and others, including the following : 

* ''[[Identity (philosophy) | Identity]]'', the fact that a feature is unique and distinct from all other features. This does not have an inherent description, but humans have created many systems for attempting to express identity, such as [[name]]s and [[Identifier | identification numbers/codes]].
* ''[[Existence]]'', the fact that a feature exists in the world. At first, this may seem trivial, but complex situations are common, such as features that are proposed or planned, abstract concepts (e.g., the [[Equator]]), under construction, or that no longer exist.
* ''[[Natural kind | Kind]]'' (also known as class, type, or category), one or more groups to which a feature belongs, typically focused on those that are most fundamental to its existence.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mark |first1=David M. |last2=Smith |first2=Barry |last3=Tversky |first3=Barbara |editor1-last=Freksa |editor1-first=Christian |editor2-last=Mark |editor2-first=Davis M. |title=Spatial Information Theory: A Theoretical Basis for GIS (COSIT '99), Lecture Notes in Computer Science #1661 |date=1999 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=Berlin |isbn=978-3-540-48384-7 |pages=283–298 |chapter=Ontology and Geographic Objects: an empirical study of cognitive categorization|doi=10.1007/3-540-48384-5_19|url=https://philarchive.org/rec/MAROAG-3 }}</ref> It thus completes the sentence "This is a _________." These are generally in the form of common nouns (tree, dog, building, county, etc.), which may be isolated or part of a [[Taxonomy|taxonomic hierarchy]].
* ''[[Relations (philosophy) | Relationships]]'' to other features. These may be ''inherent'' if they are crucial to the existence and identity of the feature, or ''incidental'' if they are not crucial, but "just happen to be." These may be of at least three types:
** ''[[Spatial relation]]s'', those that can be visualized and measured in space. For example, the fact that the [[Potomac River]] is ''adjacent'' to [[Maryland]] is an inherent spatial relation because the river is part of the definition of the boundary of Maryland, but the ''overlap'' relation between Maryland and the [[Delmarva Peninsula]] is incidental, as each would exist unproblematically without the other.
** ''[[Meronomy|Meronomic relations]]'' (also known as partonomy), in which a feature may exist as a part of a larger whole, or may exist as a collection of parts. For example, the relationship between [[Maryland]] and the [[United States]] is a meronomic relation; one is not just spatially within the boundaries of the other, but is a component part of the other that in part defines the existence of both.
** ''[[Genealogy|Genealogical relations]]'' (also known as parent-child), which tie a feature to others that existed previously and created it (or from which it was formed by another agent), and in turn to any features it has created. For example, if a county were created by the subdivision of two existing counties, they would be considered its ''parents''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hornsby |first1=Kathleen |last2=Egenhofer |first2=Max J. |title=Identity-based change: a foundation for spatio-temporal knowledge representation |journal=International Journal of Geographical Information Science |date=2000 |volume=14 |issue=3 |pages=207–224 |doi=10.1080/136588100240813|bibcode=2000IJGIS..14..207H |s2cid=52861923 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* ''[[Location]]'', a description of where the feature exists, often including the shape of its extent.<ref name="huisman">{{cite book |last1=Huisman |first1=Otto |last2=de By |first2=Rolf A. |title=Principles of Geographic Information Systems |date=2009 |publisher=ITC |location=Enschede, The Netherlands |isbn=9789061642695 |page=77 |url=https://webapps.itc.utwente.nl/librarywww/papers_2009/general/principlesgis.pdf |chapter=2.2.4 Geographic objects |archive-date=2018-05-14 |access-date=2023-01-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180514113013/https://webapps.itc.utwente.nl/librarywww/papers_2009/general/principlesgis.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> While a feature has an inherent location, measuring it for the purpose of representation as data can be a complex process, such as requiring the invention of abstract [[spatial reference system]]s, and the necessary employment of [[cartographic generalization]], including an expedient choice of [[dimension]] (e.g., a city could be represented as a region or as a point, depending on scale and need).
* ''[[Variable and attribute (research)|Attributes]]'', characteristics of a feature other than location, often expressed as text or numbers; for example, the ''population'' of a city.<ref name="desmith">{{cite book |last1=de Smith |first1=Michael J. |last2=Goodchild |first2=Michael F. |last3=Longley |first3=Paul A. |title=Geospatial Analysis: A Comprehensive Guide to Principles, Techniques, and Software Tools |date=2018 |edition=6th |url=https://spatialanalysisonline.com/|chapter=Attributes|chapter-url=https://www.spatialanalysisonline.com/HTML/index.html?attributes.htm}}</ref> In geography, the [[Level of measurement|levels of measurement]] developed by [[Stanley Smith Stevens]] (and further extended by others) is a common system for understanding and using attribute data.
* ''[[Time]]'' is fundamental to the representation of a feature, although it does not have independent temporal descriptions.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Song |first1=Y. |title=FC-08 - Time |url=https://gistbok.ucgis.org/bok-topics/time |website=GIS&T Body of Knowledge |publisher=UCGIS |access-date=5 January 2023}}</ref> Instead, expressions of time are attached to other characteristics, describing how they change (thus, they are analogous to [[adverb]]s in common discourse). Any of the above characteristics is ''[[Mutability | mutable]]'', with the possible exception of identity. For example, the lifespan of a feature could be considered as the temporal extent of its existence. The location of a city can change over time as [[Municipal annexation |annexation]]s expand its extent. The resident population of a country changes frequently due to [[immigration]], [[emigration]], [[birth]], and [[death]]. 

The descriptions of features (i.e., the measured values of each of the above characteristics) are typically collected in Geographic databases, such as GIS datasets, based on a variety of [[Data model (GIS) | data models]] and [[GIS file formats | file formats]], often based on the [[Vector graphics | vector logical model]].<ref name="campbell2011">{{cite book |last1=Campbell |first1=Jonathan |last2=Shin |first2=Michael |title=Essentials of Geographic Information Systems |date=2011 |publisher=Saylor Foundation |isbn=9781453321966 |url=https://saylordotorg.github.io/text_essentials-of-geographic-information-systems/s07-01-data-and-information.html |access-date=5 January 2023 |chapter=3.1 Data and Information}}</ref>
